Backup storage location

Where backups are written on this Mac. Point this at an external drive if your internal disk doesn't have enough free space for the device's backup. Leave blank to use the default (~/Cradle/working).

Restore staging location

Where a backup is copied to just before restoring it onto a device — never the backup storage location itself (see above), which restore never touches directly. A full backup can be tens of gigabytes, so point this at whichever drive actually has room if the default fills up your internal disk. Leave blank to use the default (~/Cradle/scratch).

Local backups

Every device with a backup currently sitting on this Mac — including ones you've since unplugged, replaced, or sold. Deleting one here only removes its local copy; a device's history stays visible, and any saved copy elsewhere is untouched.

How backup works

"Back Up Now" copies everything on your device — Photos, Messages, Health, Notes, Contacts, Keychain-protected data (saved passwords, Wi-Fi networks), and every app's own data — into a folder on this Mac (see "Backup storage location" under Advanced settings). That folder is the one and only copy Cradle keeps locally; there's no separate history of past backups sitting around taking up space.

The first backup of a device is slow; every one after that is fast. Your iPhone or iPad itself keeps track of what's changed since the last backup and only sends the difference — Cradle doesn't do anything special to make this happen, it's how the device's own backup protocol works. This is also why deleting the local backup (see "Local backups" below) means the next one starts over as a full, slow transfer again.

Backup protection must be turned on before the first backup. This encrypts the backup with a password you choose, and it's not optional — without it, iOS silently leaves out Keychain items, Health data, call history, and saved Wi-Fi passwords from the backup entirely. Cradle won't let a backup start until this is on.

Every backup is verified afterward — Cradle checks that the transfer actually finished, that the backup's own internal manifest opens and passes an integrity check, and that every file the manifest expects is really there on disk. A backup that fails this check is never treated as safe to restore from or copy elsewhere, no matter how far the transfer itself got.

"Save a copy to…" makes an additional copy of an already-verified backup somewhere other than this Mac — an external drive, a NAS, or cloud storage (set up under Advanced settings → Backup copies). This is what actually protects you if this computer is lost, stolen, or its drive fails; the local backup alone doesn't.

How restore works

Restore writes a backup back onto a device — either the same device it came from, or a different one (for example, setting up a replacement iPhone with your old one's data). It erases everything currently on the target device first. There's no way to restore only part of a backup or pick and choose what comes back — the underlying device protocol only knows how to restore everything at once.

Before anything starts, Cradle checks that the target device is actually ready: it's paired and trusted, Find My is turned off (Settings → [your name] → Find My → Find My iPhone), the target's iOS version isn't older than the backup's, and the target device actually has enough free space for what's about to be written to it. If any of these would clearly fail, restore refuses to start rather than fail partway through.

You can restore from the backup already sitting on this Mac, or from a saved copy at one of your archive destinations — useful when the original local backup is gone (a different computer, a wiped drive) but a copy was saved elsewhere. Picking an archived copy lets you choose a specific past point in time, since local backups only ever reflect the most recent state.

Restoring onto a device that's still mid-setup (the "Apps & Data" screen during Setup Assistant) can work, but only once the device has gotten far enough through activation for iOS to enable its backup/restore service — pairing succeeding early doesn't guarantee that part is ready yet.

What doesn't come back automatically

Third-party apps don't reinstall themselves after a restore, and their data may not come back either — this is a real limitation, not a bug Cradle can fix with a setting. Backups have never contained the actual app files (only Apple's own apps are built into iOS itself), and the mechanism every non-Apple backup tool uses to ask iOS to redownload and reattach the rest has a long-standing, unresolved gap that affects every tool built the same way Cradle is — including the more actively maintained alternatives, and by commercial competitors' own admission in their documentation.

In practice: after a restore, expect to see only Apple's own apps at first. Reinstalling a third-party app from the App Store afterward may bring its data back if the app was already installed before the restore ran — but this isn't guaranteed. Everything else — Photos, Messages, Health, Notes, Contacts, Keychain items, and each app's saved data once reinstalled — restores reliably.

See the project's README ("Known limitations") for the full technical writeup, including what was actually tested and why this isn't fixable by a flag or a code change.
